**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 35, verses 3–7:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, remember the favor of Allah upon you.﴾ The exegetes (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir, the science of Qur'anic exegesis) said: the address is to the people of Makkah. The word ﴿remember﴾ (اذْكُرُوا) here means "guard" (احْفَظُوا). The favor of Allah upon them is that He settled them in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) and protected them from raids.

﴿Is there any creator other than Allah﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "غَيْرِ اللَّهِ" with a kasra on the ra'. Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) said: they made it an adjective following the wording (عَلى اللَّفْظِ), and this is good because it agrees with the preceding genitive (لِإتْباعِ الجَرِّ). This is an interrogative of affirmation and rebuke (istifham taqrir wa tawbikh). The meaning is: there is no creator besides Him. ﴿He provides for you from the sky﴾, meaning rain, and from ﴿the earth﴾, meaning plants. What follows has already been explained (al-An'am: 95; Ali 'Imran: 184; al-Baqarah: 210; Luqman: 33), up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you﴾, meaning he wants your destruction. ﴿So take him as an enemy﴾, meaning regard him as you would regard enemies, and avoid obeying him. ﴿He only invites his party﴾, meaning his followers, to disbelief, ﴿so that they will be among the companions of the Blaze﴾.

(p-475) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good...?﴾ Scholars differ regarding whom this verse was revealed about, in three opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and the polytheists of Makkah. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it concerns the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa') and the sects (al-milal) that deviated from guidance. This is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: they are the Jews, the Christians and the Magians. This is related from Abu Qilabah.

If it is asked: where is the answer (jawab) to ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him...?﴾

The answer is given in two ways, which al-Zajjaj mentioned.

The first: the answer is omitted, and the meaning is: "Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him like one whom Allah has guided?!" This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.﴾

The second: the meaning is: "Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, and whom Allah has led astray, [such that] your soul would go out after them in regrets?!" This is indicated by His saying: ﴿So do not let your soul expire in regret over them.﴾

(p-476) Abu Ja'far recited: "fa-la tudhhib" with a dammah on the ta' and a kasrah on the ha', and "nafsaka" with a fathah on the sin (فَلا تُذْهِبْ نَفْسَكَ بِنَصْبِ السِّينِ).

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not grieve, and do not destroy yourself through regret over their refusal of faith."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then it stirs up clouds﴾, i.e., it drives them from their place. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it gathers them and brings them. ﴿We drive it﴾ means "We drive it" (nasuquhu). The Arabs sometimes place "fa'alna" in the position of "naf'alu," and they recited:

"If they hear a doubtful matter, they fly with it in joy at me, and if they hear of something good, they bury it."

The meaning: "yatiru" and "yadfinu" (they would fly and they would bury).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus is the resurrection﴾, which is life. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of this statement.

The first: just as Allah revives the earth after its death, so Allah will revive the dead on the Day of Resurrection. "Abu Razin al-'Uqayli related, saying: I said: O Messenger of Allah, how does Allah revive the dead, and what is the sign of that in His creation? He said: 'Have you passed by the valley of your family when it was barren, then you passed by it while it was green and stirring?' I said: Yes. He said: 'Thus does Allah revive the dead, and that is His sign in His creation.'"

The second: just as Allah revived the dead earth with water, so Allah revives the dead with water.

(p-477) Ibn Mas'ud said: "Allah, Exalted is He, sends water from beneath the Throne like the semen of men. He said: their flesh and bodies grow from that water, just as the earth grows from moist soil. Then he recited this verse." We have already mentioned a similar explanation in (al-A'raf: 57).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 35, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever desires honor﴾ — there are three opinions concerning it.

The first: whoever desires honor through the worship of idols, then ﴿to God belongs all honor﴾. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: whoever desires honor, let him seek honor through obedience to God. This is the view of Qatada. Anas has related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Your Lord says every day: I am the Mighty (al-'Aziz). So whoever desires the honor of both abodes, let him obey the Mighty."

The third: whoever desires honor, to whom it belongs — it belongs entirely to God. This is the view of al-Farra'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Nakha'i, al-Jahdari, and al-Shaizari, on the authority of al-Kisa'i, recited (p-478) "yas'adu al-kalamu al-tayyibu" (the good speech ascends), and it is His declaring of His oneness and His remembrance. ﴿And righteous deed raises it﴾. 'Ali ibn al-Madini said: the good word is "There is no god but God," and the righteous deed is performing the obligatory duties and avoiding the forbidden things.

Concerning the pronoun of reference in His saying ﴿raises it﴾, there are three opinions.

The first: it refers back to the good word. The meaning is: righteous deed raises the good word. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. Al-Hasan used to say: speech is presented to action; if the speech agrees with the action it is accepted, and if it contradicts it, it is rejected.

The second: it refers back to the righteous deed. The meaning is: the good word raises the righteous deed. This is the reverse of the first opinion, and it is the view of Abu Salih and Shahr ibn Hawshab. If we say that the good word is monotheism, the benefit of this view is that no righteous deed is accepted except from one who is a monotheist.

The third: it refers back to God, the Mighty and Majestic. The meaning is: righteous deed is raised by God to Himself, i.e., He accepts it. This is the view of Qatada.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who plot evil deeds﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "yamkurun" (they plot) means "yaktasibun" (they earn) and "yajtarihun" (they commit). Then, concerning those referred to, there are four opinions. (p-479) The first: they are those who plotted against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the Dar al-Nadwa. This is the view of Abu al-'Aliya.

The second: they are the people of showing off (riya'). This is the view of Mujahid and Shahr ibn Hawshab.

The third: they are those who commit evil deeds. This is the view of Qatada and Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The fourth: they are those who utter polytheism. This is the view of Muqatil.

Concerning the meaning of ﴿yabur﴾ (will perish), there are two opinions. The first: it means "yubtilu" (it will be void), the view of Ibn Qutayba. The second: it means "yafsadu" (it will be corrupted), the view of al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 35, verse 11–14:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah created you from dust﴾, meaning Adam, ﴿then from a sperm-drop﴾, meaning his offspring, ﴿then He made you into pairs﴾, that is, kinds: males and females. Qatadah said: He paired some of them with others.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And no one is granted a lifespan or has it shortened﴾, that is, no one's life is lengthened. Al-Hasan and Ya'qub read "yunqasu" with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the qaf. ﴿of his lifespan﴾ — regarding this pronoun (ha') there are two views.

One: it is a reference to another person, so the meaning is: "nor is anything subtracted from the lifespan of another." This meaning is in the narration of al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid and others said likewise. Al-Farra' said: It is referred to indirectly as if it were the first, because if the second noun were stated explicitly it would be like the first, as if he had said: "nor is anything subtracted from the lifespan of one who is granted a lifespan." A similar usage in speech is: "I have a dirham and its half," meaning: "and another half."

The second: it refers back to the mentioned person who is granted a lifespan. So the meaning is: no day or night passes from the lifespan of this person except that it is recorded. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: It is written at the beginning of the Book: "his lifespan is such-and-such years," then written beneath it: "one day has passed, two days have passed, three days have passed," until his lifespan ends. This meaning is in the narration of Ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Ikrimah and Abu Malik said likewise, among others.

As for the Book, it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Regarding His saying, ﴿Indeed, that is easy for Allah﴾, there are two views.

One: it refers to the recording of the terms (al-ajal). The second: it refers to the increase and decrease of the lifespan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾, meaning the sweet and the salty. This verse and what follows have already been explained (Al-Furqan: 53, An-Nahl: 14, Al-Imran: 27, Ar-Ra'd: 2), up to His saying: ﴿They do not possess even a qitmir﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: It is the thin skin that is on the back of the date-pit.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you call upon them, they do not hear your call﴾, because they are inanimate, ﴿and even if they heard﴾, by Allah creating for them ears, ﴿they would not respond to you﴾, that is, they would have no response. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your associating them with Him﴾, that is, they will disown your worship of them. ﴿And none can inform you, [O Muhammad], like one who is All-Aware﴾, that is, the Knower of things, meaning Himself, Mighty and Majestic; and the meaning is that there is no one more informed than Him, Mighty and Majestic, regarding what He has informed that will occur.

**The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 35, verses 27–28:**

His statement, may God Most High say: ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red, of varying shades, and extremely black﴾. That is: and among what We have created of the mountains are streaks (*judad*). Ibn Qutayba said: *judad* are the lines and strips found in mountains, some of them white, some of them red, and some of them *gharabib* jet-black. *Gharabib* is the plural of *ghirbib*, which means the intensely black, as in the expression *aswad ghirbib* ("intensely black"). The sentence is complete at His words ﴿thus﴾, meaning: among the mountains are those of differing colours, ﴿and among people, animals and cattle are those of differing colours, likewise﴾, that is, like the variation of the fruits. Al-Farra' said: there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*) in the sentence; its intended form is *wa sud gharabib* ("and black, intensely black"), because it is said *aswad ghirbib*, and it is rarely said *ghirbib aswad*. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "and among the mountains are *gharabib sud*," and these are the ones with black rock. Ibn Durayd said: *ghirbib* means black; I think its derivation is from *ghurab* (crow).

The exegetes differ on the meaning of *gharabib* in three ways:

First: the black streaks; this was said by Ibn Abbas. Second: the black valleys; this was said by Qatada. Third: the black mountains; this was said by al-Suddi.

Then He began, saying: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾, meaning: those who have knowledge of God, Mighty and Majestic. Ibn Abbas said: He means, only those among My creation fear Me who know My majesty, My might and My sovereignty. Mujahid and al-Sha'bi said: the one who has knowledge is the one who fears God. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: whoever does not fear God is not a person of knowledge.

The first: they are the Community of Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are the Prophets and their followers. This was said by al-Hasan.

(p-488) Regarding "the Book" there are two views.

The first: it is a generic noun, and what is meant by it is the Books which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down. This is derived from the two views above. If we say that those who were chosen are the Community of Muhammad, then Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah caused the Community of Muhammad (ﷺ) to inherit every Book He sent down. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: The meaning of that is that He caused them to inherit faith in all the Books, and all the Books enjoin following the Qur'an, so they believe in them and act upon their requirements. He supported the soundness of this view by the fact that Allah, Exalted, said in the verse before this: ﴿And that which We have revealed to you of the Book is the truth﴾, and followed it with His saying: ﴿Then We caused the Book to be inherited﴾. The second view: what is meant by the Book is the Qur'an.

The first: "a'taynā" (We gave), because inheritance is a gift. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: "akhkharnā" (We delayed), and from it comes "al-mirath" (inheritance), because it comes after the deceased. So the meaning is: We delayed the Qur'an beyond the earlier nations and gave it to this Community, honouring it. This was mentioned by some of the scholars of meanings.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 35, verses 40–41:**

[p. 496] His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you seen your partners whom you invoke besides Allah?﴾ The meaning is: Tell me about those you worshipped besides Allah and took as partners by your own claim. By what did you make them deserving of a share in worship? Did they create anything of the earth, or did they share with the Creator of the heavens in creating them? Then he returned to the disbelievers and said: ﴿Or have We given them a Book, so that they stand upon clear proof from it?﴾ That is, a Book commanding them to do what they do. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read *bayyinatin* (clear proof) in the singular, indicating tawhid (the singular form). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read *bayyinat* (clear proofs) in the plural. The intended meaning is a clear demonstration that there is a partner with Allah. ﴿Nay, the wrongdoers promise one another nothing but delusion﴾: that is, the polytheists promise one another that the idols will intercede for them, and that there will be no reckoning or punishment for them. Muqatil said: Satan promises the disbelievers nothing but falsehood regarding the intercession of the gods.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease [to exist]﴾: that is, He prevents them from ceasing, from departing, and from falling. Al-Farra' said: *wa-la'in* (and if indeed) here means *wa-law* (and even if), and *in* means *ma* (not), so the sense is: even if they were to cease, no one could hold them back. Al-Zajjaj said: When the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and the Jews said, "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," the heavens nearly split apart, the mountains nearly collapsed, and the earth nearly cracked open; but Allah, mighty and majestic, held them. He used the singular *al-ard* (the earth) alongside the plural *al-samawat* (the heavens) because *al-ard* indicates the earths. ﴿And if they should cease﴾ allows two interpretations. The first: their ceasing will occur on the Day of Resurrection. The second: it is put hypothetically, as though to say, "And even if they did not cease." This is a context that points to power, but He mentioned forbearance in it, because when He held them back at their saying, ﴿The Most Merciful has taken a son﴾ [Maryam: 88], He showed forbearance and did not hasten punishment upon them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by Allah with their most solemn oaths﴾. He means the disbelievers of Makkah, who swore by Allah before the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, if a warner (nadhir) came to them﴾, i.e., the Messenger of Allah, ﴿they would surely be better guided than any (one of) the nations﴾, i.e., more correct in religion, ﴿than any (one of) the nations﴾, meaning the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians. ﴿But when a warner came to them﴾, namely Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿it increased them in nothing except aversion﴾, i.e., distance from guidance, ﴿in arrogance upon the earth﴾, i.e., transgression against Allah and arrogance in refusing to believe in Him.
